prompt: Each company below splits its market in one way. Is it segmenting geographically or demographically?

cards.text: A tire maker sells snow tires in Québec and all-season tires in British Columbia.
cards.explanation: Québec and British Columbia are geographical units (provinces), so the market is divided by place.

cards.text: A bank offers one account for university students and another for retirees.
cards.explanation: Students and retirees differ in age and life-cycle stage, which are demographic variables.

cards.text: A coffee chain changes its menu for each Montréal neighborhood, from the Plateau to Saint-Laurent.
cards.explanation: Neighborhoods are the smallest geographical unit on the slide.

cards.text: A travel company designs one tour for baby boomers and a different one for Gen Z.
cards.explanation: Baby boomers and Gen Z are generations, one of the demographic variables.

cards.text: A car brand aims its top model at households earning over $250,000 a year.
cards.explanation: The company divides buyers by income, a demographic variable.

cards.text: A phone company runs one plan for big cities and another for rural counties.
cards.explanation: Cities and counties are geographical units, so this is geographic segmentation.

prompt: A sportswear brand segments its buyers by behavior. Which variable is it using in each case?

cases.text: It runs a campaign in the weeks before the Montréal marathon, when runners buy new shoes.
cases.explanation: The campaign is timed to a moment when people buy, so it segments by occasion.

cases.text: It sells one shoe line to buyers who want cushioning and another to buyers who want speed.
cases.explanation: Cushioning and speed are the benefits people look for, so this is segmenting by benefits sought.

cases.text: It sends a guide to people who have never bought running gear before.
cases.explanation: The group is non-users, or first-time users, so it segments by user status.

cases.text: It offers a discount to runners who wear out three pairs of shoes a year.
cases.explanation: These buyers use a lot of the product, so the variable is usage rate.

cases.text: It invites customers who have bought only its brand for five years to an early sale.
cases.explanation: These buyers keep coming back to the brand, so they are grouped by loyalty status.

cases.text: It creates gift sets that go on sale only in December.
cases.explanation: The December holidays are an occasion for buying, so this segments by occasion.

prompt: A Canadian snack company is weighing new segments. Which of the three factors does each finding speak to?

cases.text: Sales of gluten-free snacks have grown every year for the past five years.
cases.explanation: How big a segment is and how fast it grows is the first factor, segment size and growth.

cases.text: Three large, aggressive rivals already fight over the protein-bar segment.
cases.explanation: Many strong and aggressive competitors make a segment less attractive in its structure.

cases.text: The company has no factory that can bake fresh bread, which the bakery segment requires.
cases.explanation: The company lacks the skills and resources to succeed there, so this is about its own objectives and resources.

cases.text: Anyone with a kitchen and a website can start selling homemade granola.
cases.explanation: When it is easy for new entrants to come in, the segment is structurally less attractive.

cases.text: Only a few hundred people in the country buy insect-protein chips.
cases.explanation: A very small segment fails on size and growth.

cases.text: Its five-year plan is to become known for healthy snacks for children.
cases.explanation: What the company wants to achieve is its objectives, the third factor.

prompt: A laptop maker is choosing which differences to promote. Each difference below fails one test. Which one?

cases.text: The logo on the lid comes in 40 colours, but buyers say they do not care about it.
cases.explanation: A difference must deliver a benefit buyers value. This one does not matter to them.

cases.text: Its laptops charge through USB-C, just like every other laptop on the shelf.
cases.explanation: Every competitor offers the same thing, so it is not distinctive.

cases.text: It claims fast start-up, but a rival's laptop starts up twice as fast.
cases.explanation: Other ways to get the same benefit are better, so the difference is not superior.

cases.text: A new cooling chip works well, but buyers cannot see or feel what it does.
cases.explanation: If buyers cannot see the difference or have it explained to them, it is not communicable.

cases.text: Its thin design could be copied by rivals within two months.
cases.explanation: Competitors can copy it easily, so the difference is not preemptive.

cases.text: A gold-plated edition is lovely, but it doubles the price for buyers.
cases.explanation: Buyers cannot afford to pay for the difference, so it is not affordable.

cases.text: Free lifetime repairs would cost the company more than it earns on each laptop.
cases.explanation: The company cannot make money on this difference, so it is not profitable.

prompt: Compare each brand with its rivals. Match each value proposition to the brand that offers it.

pairs.match: A hotel offers butlers, silk sheets and a rooftop spa, and charges three times the price of other hotels.
pairs.explanation: More benefits at a higher price is More for More.

pairs.match: A grocery store brand of cereal tastes the same as the leading brand and costs 30% less.
pairs.explanation: The same benefits at a lower price is The Same for Less.

pairs.match: An airline drops free bags, meals and seat choice, and sells its tickets at a fraction of the usual fare.
pairs.explanation: Fewer benefits for a much lower price is Less for much Less.

pairs.match: A car brand adds heated seats and a longer warranty but keeps its price level with its rivals.
pairs.explanation: More benefits at the same price is More for the Same.

pairs.match: A new phone has a better camera and longer battery than the market leader, yet costs less.
pairs.explanation: More benefits at a lower price is More for Less.
